paragraphs.heading: Pushing at the right rhythm
paragraphs.text: Resonance happens when a system is shaken by an outside force or vibration that repeats at one of the system's resonant frequencies, meaning a frequency at which the system responds most strongly. The system then takes in energy from the force and vibrates with a bigger amplitude, or size of swing. Even small, regular pushes close to a resonant frequency can build up very large oscillations, because the system stores the energy of vibration.

paragraphs.heading: The playground swing
paragraphs.text: A playground swing is a familiar example, since it behaves like a pendulum. Push someone in time with the swing's own natural rhythm and the swing climbs higher and higher. Push faster or slower than that rhythm and the arcs stay smaller. The swing takes in the most energy when the pushes line up with its natural back-and-forth motion.

paragraphs.heading: Storing and trading energy
paragraphs.text: Resonance needs a system that can store energy and pass it easily between two or more forms, such as kinetic energy and potential energy in a swinging pendulum. Some energy leaks away on every cycle, and this loss is called damping. Every system tends to vibrate at a natural frequency, the rate of its unforced vibrations, which depends on how it is built. When damping is small, the resonant frequency sits very close to the natural frequency, though in general the two are not exactly the same.

paragraphs.heading: Finding the peaks
paragraphs.text: Drive a system with a smooth, wave-like input and some measured output may start to oscillate in response. The ratio between the size of the output's steady swings and the size of the input's swings is called the gain, and it can change with the input's frequency. Peaks in the gain mark resonances, where the output swings far more than its share. Some systems have several separate resonant frequencies.

paragraphs.heading: What damping does
paragraphs.text: For a damped mass on a spring, resonance means the mass moves far from its resting point at certain driving frequencies. Its swing is biggest at the driving frequency ω_r = ω₀√(1 − 2ζ²), where ω₀ is the undamped angular frequency and ζ is the damping ratio. So the resonant frequency is not the same as ω₀; the two match only if the damping ratio goes to zero. This peak exists only when ζ < 1/√2, so the system can resonate only if it is strongly underdamped. With very little damping and a drive close to the resonant frequency, the steady oscillations can grow very large.

paragraphs.heading: Useful and harmful
paragraphs.text: Resonance occurs with every type of vibration or wave, from mechanical and acoustic resonance to orbital, electromagnetic and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). It is often wanted in certain uses, such as musical instruments or radio receivers. Resonant systems can produce vibrations of one chosen frequency, as instruments do, or pick particular frequencies out of a jumble of many, as filters do. But resonance can also do damage, causing too much vibration or even making structures fail.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word comes from
paragraphs.text: The word comes from the Latin resonantia, 'echo', from resonare, 'resound'. It began in acoustics, which Galileo Galilei discussed in his book Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences. The case in view was above all sympathetic resonance in musical instruments, where striking one string sets a different string vibrating and sounding.
